notes.text: The money — The price of land was strangely fallen at this time, when the enemy was besieging the chief city of the country.

I took — It is probable, that upon such sales among the Jews, two instruments were made, the one sealed up, to be kept by the purchaser, the other open, to be shewed to the Judges, and by them ratified.

Baruch — This Baruch (chap. xlvi, 4, 26,) was a scribe, and an attendant upon Jeremiah. Witnesses - He made this purchase with all the usual formalities; he signed and sealed it before witnesses, and delivered it to Baruch to keep, in the presence of all the Jews.

glossa.text: *The word which,* etc. ((HIER.)) Not only the words, but also *sedet* the works of the prophets are to us for examples of the virtues. Jeremias could have announced prosperous things and enjoyed the friendship of the king, but he chose rather to obey God, who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.

*In the court of the prison. ((ID.))* The clemency on the king's part is to be noted, who had commanded that he be shut up not in the prison, but in the vestibule of the prophets, that is to say in free custody, lest he should be able to escape; as though all Jerusalem, shut in with fortifications, had not been a common prison.

*For he had shut him up.* The captivity being now *Jean* at hand, the city being now consumed with pestilence and famine, and yet Sedecias persists in his sentence.

*Why dost thou prophesy.* Heavier is the terror before the rebuke of words, than to bear the torment of punishments, and to see him whom thou fearest.

*Behold Hanameel, the son.* Helchias and Sellum, etc., *as far as* the beginning of this volume shows.

*Buy thee a field.* That field is priestly, whose purchase and possession is committed to Jeremias, and it is in Anathot in the land of Benjamin. Of which names the first sounds obedience, the second the son of the right hand; and fittingly he seeks the purchase of that in which the obedience and the power of the Lord was engaged.
*In the land of Benjamin. ((ID.))* That is, of the suburban lands, etc., *as far as* Let them hear who attempt to claim false things by bringing forward witnesses.
*And I commanded Baruch. ((ID.))* Baruch, who is interpreted *blessed,* etc., *as far as* let him show an open volume to those desiring to read this.
*In an earthen vessel,* etc. Lest, being placed outside, they should lie open to plunder, etc., *as far as* yet they are moved by the word of God.
*Houses and fields shall still be possessed.* This is what Jeremias said above, that he had understood the word of God, and had therefore bought the field.

notes.text: He — He that makes God his habitation and refuge.
Pestilence — From the pestilence, which like a fowler's snare takes men suddenly and unexpectedly.

By night — When evil accidents are most terrible and least avoidable. Arrow - The pestilence, or any such destructive calamity; such are frequently called God's arrows. By day - Thou shalt be kept from secret and open mischiefs.
Darkness — Invisibly, so that we can neither foresee nor prevent it.

Because — This and the two following verses are the words of God. God is praised for his works, ver. 1-5. The doom of the wicked, from the eternal God, ver. 6-9. The prosperity of the righteous, ver. 10-15. A psalm or song for the sabbath-day.

glossa.text:
*The praise of a canticle.* Praise is human also: but this praise is of a canticle, because it is nothing if not divine. For this psalm is a hymn against the demons. The Prophet therefore says of any holy man whatsoever: *He that dwelleth in the help,* etc.

((CASS.)) He shows that the temptations of the devil were overcome through humility by Christ, and by his own, who remain in the help of God, that we too through him may learn to overcome temptations, because he is the door through which *jauna*, if any man shall enter in, he shall go in, and shall go out, and pasture shall come forth.

((AUG.)) Christ is the door; to enter through him is to imitate him, not in godhead, and power, and miracles, but in that wherein he was made for us, that is, in the humility to which he calls, saying: *Learn of me, because I am meek and humble of heart.* Out of this psalm the devil tempted Christ. But Christ's temptation is our teaching, and following him we overcome by him.

*He that dwelleth.* ((CASS.)) He describes first the man who trusts in God alone, wholly walled about by the protection of God. *He that dwelleth,* that is, who sets all his hope always not in himself, but in God, shall be protected by God in every way. Note the correspondence of the words: for as he always *dwelleth,* so also shall he always *abide.* The one he affirms, namely that he *dwelleth;* the other he promises, namely that he *shall be protected.*

*He shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven.* That is to say, that he turn not aside to the right hand or to the left, as in the Old Testament it was commanded to the children of Israel, that they should walk by the king's highway, not turning aside to the right hand or to the left. The king's highway is the way of Christ our king, who so ran the way of the world that he was neither enticed by prosperity, nor broken by adversity.

*My God.* ((CASS.)) Lest thou think that after the upholding and the refuge nothing further is to be asked for, he adds: *In him will I trust,* lest at any time he presume of himself; and if Adam had done this, he would have stood well.

*From the snare.* ((ID.)) Temptation, either by deeds, which is here called *a snare;* or by words, which is here called *a sharp word;* as if to say, even though it seem light, yet it is a grave thing to be tempted by a word. *A snare,* the craftiness of spiritual or of carnal enemies; *a sharp word,* every saying which moves a man from the divine rules. ((AUG.)) *From the snare of the hunters,* that is, of the demons, who set their snares not in the way, Christ, but round about it, to the right hand or to the left. Into these some fall even through a sharp word, as they who will not be Christ's because of those who insult the Christian name, and they who fear the detractions of men, so that they cease from the way of God.

*With his shoulders.* ((AUG., CASS.)) To him that hopes he promises the benefits of God. *The shoulders* are the workings of wonders, by which, as by arms, the power of God is shown. *The feathers* are the counsels of the Prophets, which carry men to the heavens.

 *He will overshadow.* That neither the sun of the godhead, nor the moon of the humanity, may scorch thee. *In the feathers* is the protection. *With his shoulders.* Elsewhere, *Between the shoulders.* ((AUG.)) That is, he places thee before his breast, etc., *as far as* that we may hope under his wings.

*The truth.* ((ID.)) It is God's, who does not regard persons, nor mingle those who hope in themselves with those who hope in God, but discerns the humble or the proud. ((CASS.)) Or the truth is the incarnation of Christ, whence: *Out of the earth truth is sprung ((Psal. LXXXIV))*, which both overshadows with the shoulders, and defends with the shield. As he has noted the kinds of defence, so he notes also the kinds of dangers, that the deliverance may be the more welcome.

*From the fear of the night.* From the likeness of a danger, whence only fear is had. *From the fear of the night.* ((AUG.)) He who sins in ignorance, etc., *as far as: A thousand shall fall at thy side.*

*Because he hoped in me.* ((AUG.)) Thirdly, the words of God, by which he consoles the Church, to which he promises both defence here, and rewards in the world to come. ((CASS.)) He gives charge to the angels concerning thee, saying: *Because in me.* The certainty of the promise, through the promise of God.
*He shall cry to me.* ((AUG.)) There is no need to fear in tribulation, etc., *as far as* at that time let us labour the more to resist.

notes.text: But godliness with content — The inseparable companion of true, vital religion. Is great gain - Brings unspeakable profit in time, as well as eternity.
Neither can we carry anything out — To what purpose, then, do we heap together so many things? O, give me one thing, - a safe and ready passage to my own country!
Covering — That is, raiment and an house to cover us. This is all that a Christian needs, and all that his religion allows him to desire.

They that desire to be rich — To have more than these; for then they would be so far rich; and the very desire banishes content, and exposes them to ruin. Fall-plunge - A sad gradation! Into temptation - Miserable food for the soul! And a snare - Or trap. Dreadful "covering!" And into many foolish and hurtful desires - Which are sown and fed by having more than we need. Then farewell all hope of content! What then remains, but destruction for the body, and perdition for the soul?

Love of money — Commonly called "prudent care" of what a man has. Is the root - The parent of all manner of evils. Which some coveting have erred - Literally, missed the mark. They aimed not at faith, but at something else. And pierced themselves with many sorrows - From a guilty conscience, tormenting passions, desires contrary to reason, religion, and one another. How cruel are worldly men to themselves!

But thou, O man of God — Whatever all the world else do. A man of God is either a prophet, a messenger of God, or a man devoted to God; a man of another world. Flee - As from a serpent, instead of coveting these things. Follow after righteousness - The whole image of God; though sometimes this word is used, not in the general, but in the particular, acceptation, meaning only that single branch of it which is termed justice. Faith - Which is also taken here in the general and full sense; namely, a divine, supernatural sight of God, chiefly in respect of his mercy in Christ. This faith is the foundation of righteousness, the support of godliness, the root of every grace of the Spirit. Love - This St. Paul intermixes with everything that is good: he, as it were, penetrates whatever he treats of with love, the glorious spring of all inward and outward holiness.

Fight the good fight of faith — Not about words. Lay hold on eternal life - Just before thee. Thou hast confessed the good confession - Perhaps at his baptism: so likewise, ver. 13; but with a remarkable variation of the expression. Thou hast confessed the good confession before many witnesses - To which they all assented. He witnessed the good confession; but Pilate did not assent to it.
I charge thee before God, who quickeneth all things — Who hath quickened thee, and will quicken thee at the great day.
Which — Appearing. In his own times - The power, the knowledge, and the Revelation of which, remain in his eternal mind.
Who only hath underived, independent immortality. Dwelling in light unapproachable — To the highest angel. Whom no man hath seen, or can see - With bodily eyes. Yet "we shall see him as he is."

What follows seems to be a kind of a postscript. Charge the rich in this world — Rich in such beggarly riches as this world affords. Not to be highminded - O who regards this! Not to think better of themselves for their money, or anything it can purchase. Neither to trust in uncertain riches - Which they may lose in an hour; either for happiness or defense. But in the living God - All the rest is dead clay. Who giveth us - As it were holding them out to us in his hand. All things - Which we have. Richly - Freely, abundantly. To enjoy - As his gift, in him and for him. When we use them thus, we do indeed enjoy all things. Where else is there any notice taken of the rich, in all the apostolic writings, save to denounce woes and vengeance upon them?

To do good — To make this their daily employ, that they may be rich - May abound in all good works. Ready to distribute - Singly to particular persons. Willing to communicate - To join in all public works of charity.

Treasuring up for themselves a good foundation — Of an abundant reward, by the free mercy of God. That they may lay hold on eternal life - This cannot be done by alms-deeds; yet they "come up for a memorial before God," Acts x, 4. And the lack even of this may be the cause why God will withhold grace and salvation from us.

glossa.text: *For they that will.* This is said to those who will and are not, that they may not desire. Now to the rich another thing is said, namely, not to be highminded, but to give to the poor. *They fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, because the root of all evils,* etc. There is no kind of evil which does not sometimes arise from covetousness, because the root of all evils is covetousness.

*Covetousness.* In the Greek there stands, φιλαργυρία. If therefore avarice, which properly is the love of money, is taken in place of the genus which is covetousness, a species is put.

*With many sorrows.* For the avaricious sustain the torment of anxiety so much the more, the more they desire the things which either, being had, pass away, or which they cannot have.

*But thou, man,* etc. He does not say that he fears this concerning that man, but he knew that this would come into the hands of the churches. *Flee these things.* For nothing is so harsh and so pernicious as if an ecclesiastical man, and most of all he who holds a lofty place, should give study to the riches of this world: because he harms not only himself but also the rest, to whom he gives a contrary pattern. *Piety.* Piety is that we condescend to the needy, which the covetous man does not do. *Faith.* He who has a true faith concerning God does not desire to become rich amid miseries, nor is the world of more worth to him than God.
*I charge thee.* In Timothy the Apostle speaks to all his successors. *And Christ Jesus.* By the example of Christ he exhorts.
*Blessed and only,* etc. He says this not of the Father only, but of God who is the Trinity itself.

*Who only hath immortality* He has it by nature, others from him by grace. *Inaccessible, whom none of men.* Because none comes to it of himself, but to whom it is given, it is given by his gift, which the Prophet understood, saying: *Come ye to him, and be enlightened ((Psal. XXXIII))*, etc.

*To the rich of this world.* Above he treated of those who wish to become rich, saying that they fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, here he treats of those who are rich, admonishing them not to hope in riches. And because he said that evils come from covetousness, and persuaded the contrary, lest the rich should seem cast off, he determines. *Not to be highminded.* The Apostle did not dread riches, but their disease, that is, pride, which is the worm of the rich. Great is the mind which among riches is not tempted with that disease. He is great who does not therefore think himself great, because he is rich. But he who therefore thinks himself great is proud, is needy, swells in the flesh, cracks in the heart, begs, is puffed up, not full. *To enjoy.* For temporal things God gives in this life to use, eternal things to enjoy: the former, whence we may do good; the latter whence we may be made good.
*To lay up in store.* Unto this are riches sent before that shall not perish.

notes.text: There was a certain rich man — Very probably a Pharisee, and one that justified himself before men; a very honest, as well as honourable gentleman: though it was not proper to mention his name on this occasion: who was clothed in purple and fine linen - and doubtless esteemed on this account, (perhaps not only by those who sold it, but by most that knew him, ) as encouraging trade, and acting according to his quality: And feasted splendidly every day - And consequently was esteemed yet more, for his generosity and hospitality in keeping so good a table.

And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, (according to the Greek pronunciation) or Eleazer. By his name it may be conjectured, he was of no mean family, though it was thus reduced. There was no reason for our Lord to conceal his name, which probably was then well known. Theophylact observes, from the tradition of the Hebrews, that he lived at Jerusalem. Yea, the dogs also came and licked his sores — It seems this circumstance is recorded to show that all his ulcers lay bare, and were not closed or bound up.

And the beggar — Worn out with hunger, and pain, and want of all things, died: and was carried by angels (amazing change of the scene!) into Abraham's bosom - So the Jews styled paradise; the place where the souls of good men remain from death to the resurrection. The rich man also died, and was buried - Doubtless with pomp enough, though we do not read of his lying in state; that stupid, senseless pageantry, that shocking insult on a poor, putrefying carcass, was reserved for our enlightened age!
He seeth Abraham afar off — And yet knew him at that distance: and shall not Abraham's children, when they are together in paradise, know each other!

Father Abraham, have mercy on me — It cannot be denied, but here is one precedent in Scripture of praying to departed saints: but who is it that prays, and with what success? Will any, who considers this, be fond of copying after him?

But Abraham said, Son — According to the flesh. Is it not worthy of observation, that Abraham will not revile even a damned soul? and shall living men revile one another? Thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things - Thou didst choose and accept of worldly things as thy good, thy happiness. And can any be at a loss to know why he was in torments? This damnable idolatry, had there been nothing more, was enough to sink him to the nethermost hell.
Beside this there is a great gulf fixed — Reader, to which side of it wilt thou go?
Lest they also come into this place — He might justly fear lest their reproaches should add to his own torment.
Neither will they be persuaded — Truly to repent: for this implies an entire change of heart: but a thousand apparitions cannot, effect this. God only can, applying his word.

glossa.text:
*A certain man.* Against the avaricious mockers he builds up by an example what he had set forth, namely that the rich man is tormented among those below, who did not make Lazarus his friend, by whom he might have been received into eternal tabernacles; and it seems rather a narrative than a parable.

*Who was clothed in purple,* etc. ((GREG.)) Purple is the colour of royal apparel, from sea-shells, etc., *as far as* because he knew nothing of the bowels of pity, because he was unwilling to redeem the precepts with a price.

*And there was a certain.* If we see anything blameworthy in the poor, we ought not to despise them, because perhaps those whom weakness of manners wounds, the medicine of poverty heals. *Full of sores.* At this man's sores the fastidious rich man shudders, lest amid precious banquets and perfumed guests he should endure the stench of sores with the dogs licking them.

*Desiring.* In one thing two judgments of God are fulfilled: from the sight of the poor man a heap of damnation is brought upon the rich man who does not pity; and again from the sight of the rich man the poor man, tempted daily, is proved, whom, for his own greater proving, poverty together with sickness, and the beheld plenty of the rich man, and no consolation applied to him, afflict. *The dogs.* In the tongue of the dogs there can be signified the tongue of flatterers who lick wounds, while with wicked favour they praise the evils which we blame in ourselves.

*Into Abraham's bosom.* Abraham's bosom is the rest of the blessed poor, whose is the kingdom of heaven, into which after this life they are received. The burial of hell is the depth of punishments, which devours the proud and the unmerciful after this life. *And he was buried.* In the law not niggardliness but rapine is condemned; in the Gospel the rich man is tormented because he did not give what was his own.

*And lifting up.* The unfaithful see afar off, while, set in the depth before the day of judgment, they mark the faithful above them in rest, whose joys afterwards they cannot behold. What they descry is far off, because they do not reach thither by merit.

*He saw Abraham. ((GREG.))* It is to be believed that before the retribution of the last judgment the unjust in rest, etc., *as far as* and they are tormented by the punishment of those whom they loved uselessly.

*That he may dip.* He who did not give to Lazarus the crumbs falling from the table, desires that water be distilled into his mouth from the tip of that man's finger; and he who gave not the least things in life, in hell seeks the least things.

*Because thou hast received. ((AUG.))* Note that this rich man had something of good, out of which he received a transitory good in this life, and Lazarus had something of evil, but the want of fire purged it.

*And in all these things.* Just as the reprobate wish to pass over from their punishments to the glory of the saints, so the just wish in mind through mercy to go to those set in torments, that they may free them; but they cannot, because the souls of the just, though in the goodness of their own nature they have mercy, are yet now joined to the righteousness of their Author and are bound with so great a rectitude that they are moved by no compassion toward the reprobate.

*I beseech thee therefore.* After hope for himself is taken from the burning man, his mind runs back to his kinsmen, because the punishment of the reprobate sometimes uselessly instructs their mind unto charity, so that then at last they love even their own spiritually, who here, while they loved their sins, did not even love themselves. There is kept therefore for the rich man unto punishment both the knowledge of the poor man whom he despised, and the memory of the brethren whom he left behind, that he may be the more tormented by the beheld glory of the despised and by the punishment of those he uselessly loved. *That thou wouldst send.* Too late does this rich man begin to be a master, when he has now neither time for learning nor for teaching.

*If Moses.* They who despise the words of the law, by how much the more subtle the precepts of the Redeemer, who rose from the dead, are, by so much the more hardly will they fulfil these, and him whose sayings they refuse to fulfil, him without doubt they refuse to believe.

echoes.text: He said, “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return there. Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh’s name.”
echoes.note: 'We brought nothing into the world, and we certainly can't carry anything out' closely renders Job's confession, 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked I will return there.' The shared logic of human poverty at birth and at death grounds the call to contentment and is the primary scriptural source for v.7.

echoes.text: As he came out of his mother’s womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, which he may carry away in his hand.
echoes.note: 'As he came from his mother's womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor.' Qoheleth's meditation on the impossibility of carrying wealth out of life is a direct conceptual parallel to v.7 and reinforces the Job allusion. The pairing forms the wisdom backbone of the contentment teaching.

echoes.text: For when he dies he shall carry nothing away. His glory shall not descend after him.
echoes.note: 'For when he dies he will carry nothing away; his glory will not descend after him.' The psalm's reflection that the rich take nothing in death directly parallels the claim that we 'can't carry anything out.' A strong supporting witness to the same death-and-dispossession tradition.

echoes.text: Set not your heart upon your goods; And say not, They are sufficient for me. Follow not your own mind and your strength, To walk in the desires of your heart; And say not, Who will have dominion over me? For the Lord will surely take vengeance on you. Say not, I sinned, and what happened to me? For the Lord is longsuffering. Concerning atonement, be not without fear, To add sin upon sins: And say not, His compassion is great; He will be pacified for the […]
echoes.note: Ben Sira warns against relying on wealth and saying 'I have enough,' urging the reader not to follow heart and strength after riches. The deuterocanonical wisdom on the futility of trusting possessions undergirds the contentment ethic of vv.6-8 and the warnings of vv.9-10.

echoes.text: Remove far from me falsehood and lies. Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me; lest I be full, deny you, and say, ‘Who is Yahweh?’ or lest I be poor, and steal, and so dishonor the name of my God.
echoes.note: Agur's prayer, 'feed me with the food that is needful for me,' seeking neither poverty nor riches, supplies the ideal of sufficiency behind 'having food and clothing, we will be content.' The wisdom request for daily necessities is the closest sapiential parallel to v.8.

echoes.text: Jacob vowed a vow, saying, “If God will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and will give me bread to eat, and clothing to put on,
echoes.note: Jacob's vow asks God for 'bread to eat and clothing to wear,' the same minimal pairing of food and clothing that defines contentment in v.8. The verbal pairing may stand behind Paul's formula, though it is a common biblical idiom of basic provision.

echoes.text: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth. Your clothing didn’t grow old on you, neither did your foot swell, these forty years.
echoes.note: The wilderness lesson that God provided manna and that clothing did not wear out teaches dependence on God for daily food and covering. This forms a faint background to the food-and-clothing sufficiency that the believer is to rest content in.

echoes.text: He who is greedy for gain troubles his own house, but he who hates bribes will live.
echoes.note: 'He who is greedy for gain troubles his own house.' The maxim that avarice brings ruin upon the grasping person directly underwrites 'the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil' and the picture of those who 'pierced themselves through with many sorrows.' A core wisdom source for v.10.

echoes.text: Many have sinned for a thing indifferent; And he that seeks to multiply gain will turn his eye away.
echoes.note: 'Many have sinned for the sake of profit, and he who seeks to multiply gain will turn his eye away.' Ben Sira's aphorism that the pursuit of money is itself a cause of sin is the closest known parallel to 'the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.' Strong deuterocanonical antecedent for v.10.

echoes.text: He that loves gold shall not be justified; And he that follows destruction shall himself have his fill of it. Many have been given over to ruin for the sake of gold; And their perdition meets them face to face. It is a stumbling block to those who sacrifice to it; And every fool shall be taken therewith.
echoes.note: 'He who loves gold will not be justified... Gold has been a stumbling block to many, and their destruction has met them face to face. It is a snare to those who are devoted to it.' The imagery of gold as a snare causing ruin parallels both the 'snare' of v.9 and the 'root of evil' of v.10. A remarkably close sapiential model.

echoes.text: He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he who loves abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.
echoes.note: 'He who loves silver shall not be satisfied with silver, nor he who loves abundance with increase.' Qoheleth's insight into the insatiability of money-love directly parallels the diagnosis of those 'determined to be rich' and 'the love of money.' A direct wisdom witness to the avarice critique.

echoes.text: Don’t weary yourself to be rich. In your wisdom, show restraint. Why do you set your eyes on that which is not? For it certainly sprouts wings like an eagle and flies in the sky.
echoes.note: 'Don't weary yourself to be rich... riches certainly sprout wings.' The warning against straining to be wealthy maps onto 'those who are determined to be rich fall into a temptation and a snare.' The fleeting, ensnaring character of riches grounds vv.9-10.

echoes.text: A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn’t know that poverty waits for him.
echoes.note: 'A stingy man hurries after riches, and doesn't know that poverty waits for him.' The proverb that the avaricious rush toward wealth only to meet ruin parallels the trajectory of those who 'fall into... ruin and destruction.' Supporting wisdom source.

echoes.text: but these lay wait for their own blood. They lurk secretly for their own lives. So are the ways of everyone who is greedy for gain. It takes away the life of its owners.
echoes.note: 'So are the ways of everyone who is greedy for gain. It takes away the life of its owners.' Wisdom's claim that greed is self-destructive, ambushing the very ones who seek it, parallels those who in greed 'pierced themselves through with many sorrows.' A self-harm motif resonant with v.10.

echoes.text: My son, be not busy about many matters: For if you meddle much, you will not be unpunished; And if you pursue, you will not overtake; And you will not escape by fleeing.
echoes.note: 'If you pursue, you will not overtake... and you will not escape by fleeing.' Ben Sira's counsel against frenetic pursuit of gain resonates with those 'determined to be rich' who fall into a snare. A faint deuterocanonical parallel.

echoes.text: This is the blessing with which Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death.
echoes.note: The address 'man of God' is the standard Hebrew Bible title for a prophet or authorized servant of God, applied to Moses ('the man of God') and frequently to figures like Elijah and Elisha. Timothy is cast in this prophetic-leadership lineage, charged to embody covenant virtue.

echoes.text: He said to him, “See now, there is in this city a man of God, and he is a man who is held in honor. All that he says comes surely to pass. Now let us go there. Perhaps he can tell us concerning our journey whereon we go.”
echoes.note: Samuel is repeatedly called 'the man of God,' establishing the title as a designation for a trusted seer who speaks for the Lord. The Pastoral epithet for Timothy draws on this same OT usage of the authorized divine spokesman.

echoes.text: He who follows after righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor.
echoes.note: 'He who follows after righteousness and kindness finds life, righteousness, and honor.' The exhortation to 'follow after righteousness... and gentleness' and so 'lay hold of eternal life' resonates with wisdom's promise that pursuing righteousness leads to life. A thematic virtue-pursuit parallel.

echoes.text: For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods, and Lord of lords, the great God, the mighty, and the awesome, who doesn’t respect persons, nor takes reward.
echoes.note: 'For Yahweh your God, he is God of gods and Lord of lords.' The doxology's title 'King of kings, and Lord of lords' (v.15) directly takes up this Deuteronomic confession of God's supremacy over all powers. The clearest verbal source for the title.

echoes.text: He said, “You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.”
echoes.note: 'You cannot see my face, for man may not see me and live.' The doxology's 'whom no man has seen, nor can see' (v.16) directly echoes God's word to Moses on the impossibility of beholding the divine face. A primary scriptural source for the invisibility motif.

echoes.text: He covers himself with light as with a garment. He stretches out the heavens like a curtain.
echoes.note: God is 'covered with light as with a garment.' 'Dwelling in unapproachable light' (v.16) draws on this hymnic image of God clothed in light. The closest scriptural antecedent for the light-dwelling description.

echoes.text: You are Yahweh, even you alone. You have made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their army, the earth and all things that are on it, the seas and all that is in them, and you preserve them all. The army of heaven worships you.
echoes.note: 'You give life to all of them' praises the one God who made and sustains all things. The charge before 'God, who gives life to all things' (v.13) echoes this confession of the Creator as life-giver to the whole creation. A direct conceptual parallel to the life-giving formula.

echoes.text: “See now that I myself am he. There is no god with me. I kill and I make alive. I wound and I heal. There is no one who can deliver out of my hand.
echoes.note: 'I kill and I make alive... there is no god with me.' God's exclusive prerogative over life and death undergirds 'God, who gives life to all things' and the doxology's stress that he 'alone has immortality.' Supports both the life-giver and sole-sovereign motifs of vv.13-16.

echoes.text: Give thanks to the God of gods; for his loving kindness endures forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords; for his loving kindness endures forever:
echoes.note: 'Give thanks to the God of gods... to the Lord of lords.' The liturgical pairing of these superlatives reinforces the 'Lord of lords' title of v.15 and its hymnic, doxological setting. A strong secondary witness alongside Deuteronomy 10:17.

echoes.text: The king answered to Daniel, and said, Of a truth your God is the God of gods, and the Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, since you have been able to reveal this secret.
echoes.note: Nebuchadnezzar confesses Daniel's God as 'God of gods, and Lord of kings.' The royal-supremacy formula praising the God who is over all kings parallels 'King of kings, and Lord of lords.' Reflects the apocalyptic vocabulary of divine kingship behind v.15.

echoes.text: The appearance of Yahweh’s glory was like devouring fire on the top of the mountain in the eyes of the children of Israel.
echoes.note: The glory of the Lord appeared 'like a devouring fire' on the mountain, inaccessible to the people. The unapproachable, blazing presence informs the 'unapproachable light' in which God dwells. A faint Sinai-theophany resonance.

echoes.text: For with you is the spring of life. In your light shall we see light.
echoes.note: 'For with you is the spring of life. In your light we will see light.' The association of God with life and with light loosely supports the doxology's coupling of the life-giver (v.13) with the God of unapproachable light (v.16). A thematic resonance rather than a citation.

echoes.text: The sun shall be no more your light by day; neither for brightness shall the moon give light to you: but Yahweh will be to you an everlasting light, and your God your glory.
echoes.note: 'Yahweh will be your everlasting light.' The eschatological depiction of God as light may faintly inform the doxology's 'unapproachable light.' A distant resonance secondary to Psalm 104:2.

echoes.text: Don’t trust in oppression. Don’t become vain in robbery. If riches increase, don’t set your heart on them.
echoes.note: 'If riches increase, don't set your heart on them.' The charge that the rich not 'have their hope set on the uncertainty of riches' closely matches the psalm's warning against fixing the heart on growing wealth. A primary source for v.17.

echoes.text: He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous shall flourish as the green leaf.
echoes.note: 'He who trusts in his riches will fall.' The contrast between trusting riches and the alternative directly parallels the command not to hope in 'the uncertainty of riches' but on the living God. A core wisdom antecedent for v.17.

echoes.text: Thus says Yahweh, Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, don’t let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, says Yahweh.
echoes.note: 'Don't let the rich man glory in his riches; but let him who glories glory in this, that he... knows me.' The redirection of the wealthy from boasting in riches to glorying in God parallels the charge that the rich not be haughty but hope on the living God. A strong source for the structure of v.17.

echoes.text: Why do you set your eyes on that which is not? For it certainly sprouts wings like an eagle and flies in the sky.
echoes.note: Riches 'certainly sprout wings, like an eagle they fly toward the sky.' The fleeting, unreliable nature of wealth grounds the phrase 'the uncertainty of riches.' A vivid wisdom image of money's instability.

echoes.text: and lest you say in your heart, “My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth.” But you shall remember Yahweh your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth; that he may establish his covenant which he swore to your fathers, as at this day.
echoes.note: 'Beware lest you say... My power and the might of my hand has gotten me this wealth. But you shall remember Yahweh your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth.' The warning against pride in self-made riches and the reminder that God is the giver parallels the charge against the haughty rich and the God 'who richly provides us with everything.'

echoes.text: He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.
echoes.note: 'He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him.' The exhortation that the rich 'be rich in good works, ready to distribute,' 'laying up in store... a good foundation against the time to come' echoes the wisdom principle that generosity to the needy is treasure stored with God. Grounds the storing-up imagery of v.19.

echoes.text: Give alms from your possessions. When you give alms, don’t let your eye be envious. Don’t turn away your face from any poor man, and the face of God won’t be turned away from you. As your possessions are, give alms of it according to your abundance. If you have little, don’t be afraid to give alms according to that little; for you lay up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity; because alms-giving delivers from death, and doesn’t allow […]
echoes.note: 'Give alms from your possessions... you will be laying up a good treasure for yourself against the day of necessity.' Tobit's almsgiving counsel that charity stores up a treasure for the day of need is a remarkably close parallel to 'laying up in store... a good foundation against the time to come' (v.19). A strong deuterocanonical source.

echoes.text: Bestow your treasure according to the commandments of the Most High; And it shall profit you more than gold. Shut up alms in your store-chambers; And it shall deliver you out of all affliction:
echoes.note: 'Lay up your treasure according to the commandments... and it will profit you more than gold. Store up almsgiving in your treasury, and it will rescue you from all affliction.' Ben Sira's image of almsgiving as treasure that delivers in the future directly parallels the rich laying up a good foundation against the time to come. Close sapiential antecedent for v.19.

echoes.text: Remove far from me falsehood and lies. Give me neither poverty nor riches. Feed me with the food that is needful for me; lest I be full, deny you, and say, ‘Who is Yahweh?’ or lest I be poor, and steal, and so dishonor the name of my God.
echoes.note: Agur's prayer against riches that lead one to deny God and against poverty that leads to theft frames wealth as spiritually perilous. This wisdom ambivalence about riches faintly supports the warning that the rich not be haughty nor trust their wealth.

echoes.text: If a poor man, one of your brothers, is with you within any of your gates in your land which Yahweh your God gives you, you shall not harden your heart, nor shut your hand from your poor brother; but you shall surely open your hand to him, and shall surely lend him sufficient for his need, which he lacks. Beware that there not be a base thought in your heart, saying, “The seventh year, the year of release, is at hand”; and your eye be evil against your […]
echoes.note: Lazarus laid 'at the gate' desiring crumbs while the rich man feasts dramatizes the Deuteronomic command not to harden the heart against the poor brother at your gate, for the poor will never cease in the land. High coherence with the covenantal gate-and-poor topos.

echoes.text: So Satan went out from the presence of Yahweh, and struck Job with painful sores from the sole of his foot to his head. He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes.
echoes.note: Lazarus 'full of sores' with dogs licking him evokes Job afflicted with sores from sole to crown, scraping himself amid loss. The shared imagery of a body covered in sores as the type of the abject sufferer gives coherent, available background.

echoes.text: For I was envious of the arrogant, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no struggles in their death, but their strength is firm. They are free from burdens of men, neither are they plagued like other men. Therefore pride is like a chain around their neck. Violence covers them like a garment. Their eyes bulge with fat. Their minds pass the limits of conceit. They scoff and speak with malice. In arrogance, they threaten oppression. They […]
echoes.note: The prospering, sumptuously clothed rich man set against the afflicted poor man echoes the psalmist's scandal at the wicked who are 'always at ease' and 'clothed with violence' while the godly suffer, resolved only at their end. Strong coherence with the reversal-of-fortunes frame that the parable will enact.

echoes.text: Woe to those who are at ease in Zion, and to those who are secure on the mountain of Samaria, the notable men of the chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel come! Go to Calneh, and see; and from there go to Hamath the great; then go down to Gath of the Philistines. are they better than these kingdoms? or is their border greater than your border? Those who put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near; Who lie on beds of […]
echoes.note: The rich man 'clothed in purple and fine linen, feasting in luxury every day' matches Amos' woe on those who lie on ivory beds, eat lambs, and feast while not grieved over ruin, who go first into exile. The prophetic indictment of callous luxury gives recurrent, coherent background.

echoes.text: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor, he will also cry out, but shall not be heard.
echoes.note: 'Whoever shuts his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard' anticipates the rich man's later unanswered cry from Hades after ignoring Lazarus at his gate. Coherence with the lex talionis of neglected mercy is real but the link is thematic, not verbal.

echoes.text: but you will go to your fathers in peace. You will be buried in a good old age.
echoes.note: Being 'carried to Abraham's bosom' and the rich man's address 'Father Abraham' draw on the patriarchal hope of being gathered to one's fathers, with Abraham as the paradigmatic destination of the righteous dead. Coherence with the gathered-to-Abraham motif is strong, though 'bosom' as the resting place is Second-Temple development.

echoes.text: If we suffer thus, Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob will receive us, and all the fathers will commend us.
echoes.note: 'Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will receive us' on the lips of the martyrs supplies the explicit Second-Temple picture of the righteous welcomed by the patriarchs after death, illuminating 'Abraham's bosom.' Availability and coherence with the post-mortem reception motif support the echo.

echoes.text: “They shall go out, and look on the dead bodies of the men who have transgressed against me: for their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched; and they will be loathsome to all mankind.”
echoes.note: The rich man's torment, flame, and anguish in Hades draws on Isaiah's closing vision of the dead whose fire is not quenched, the canonical seedbed of post-mortem fiery punishment. Coherence with the unquenched-fire judgment is high and the text was widely available.

echoes.text: The congregation of wicked men is as tow wrapped together; And the end of them is a flame of fire. The way of sinners is made smooth with stones; And at the last end thereof is the pit of Hades.
echoes.note: Ben Sira's image of the assembly of the wicked as tow set to flame and the broad road of sinners ending in Hades coheres with the flame and fixed-gulf fate of the rich man. The link is thematic to the sapiential fate-of-the-wicked topos rather than verbal.

echoes.text: [source text not in the World English Bible]
echoes.note: Enoch's tour of the hollow places of the dead, where the righteous and wicked are separated by a great division awaiting judgment, parallels the great chasm fixed between Lazarus and the rich man. As pseudepigraphal background to Second-Temple afterlife topography it is warranted but faint and contested.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him. This is according to all that you desired of Yahweh your God in Horeb in the day of the assembly, saying, “Let me not hear again the voice of Yahweh my God, neither let me see this great fire any more, that I not die.” Yahweh said to me, “They have well said that which they have spoken. I will raise them up a prophet from among their […]
echoes.note: 'They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them' presses the Deuteronomic demand to heed the words spoken in God's name, with refusal entailing accountability. Coherence with the obligation to 'hear' the authoritative Mosaic word is strong, framing the sufficiency-of-Scripture point.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]
echoes.note: Abraham's verdict that those who will not hear Moses will not be persuaded even by a resurrection coheres with Deuteronomy's insistence that the word is not far off in heaven or beyond reach but near, in mouth and heart, so no extraordinary sign is needed. The sufficiency and nearness of the revealed word grounds the saying.

echoes.text: Yet Yahweh testified to Israel, and to Judah, by every prophet, and every seer, saying, “Turn from your evil ways, and keep my commandments and my statutes, according to all the law which I commanded your fathers, and which I sent to you by my servants the prophets.” Notwithstanding, they would not listen, but hardened their neck, like the neck of their fathers, who didn’t believe in Yahweh their God.
echoes.note: Israel's stiff-necked refusal to listen to the LORD's testimony 'by every prophet' despite warnings prefigures brothers who 'will not be persuaded' though warned by Moses and the prophets. The recurrent prophetic-rejection motif gives coherence, but the connection is thematic rather than verbal.

notes.text: At ease — That neither fear nor believe the threatened judgments of God. In Zion - That is put for the kingdom of the two tribes, and principally the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Samaria - Woe to them also who rely upon the strength, wealth, and policy of the kingdom of Samaria or Israel. Which - Which two cities, Zion and Samaria. Named chief - Accounted the chief cities of that part of the world. To whom - To which place all Israel had recourse, the two tribes to Zion, the ten tribes to Samaria.
That lie — That out of laziness or luxury, lay themselves to rest. And eat - The very best in all their flock.
That chant — That in a time of deep mourning entertain themselves with songs, and musical instruments.

In bowls — Not in little vessels, but probably bowls: they drank these filled as full as they could hold too, and in design to drink each other down. And anoint - In those hot countries this anointing was much used. Not grieved - Nothing affected with the calamities of their country.
The banquet — The feastings of voluptuous ones shall cease.
That day — As soon as ever he is dead. Thoughts - All his designs and endeavours either for himself or for others.

For ever — Both because he liveth forever to fulfil his promises, and because he is eternally faithful. The psalmist praises God for his care over the church, ver. 1-14. His government over all, ver. 15-18. His giving his word to Israel, ver. 19, 20.

glossa.text: *Alleluia.* ((CAS.)) This voice, as it were saving musics *musicas*; read *musica*, "a saving music", like a heavenly harmony, which delights not men only but angels also, setting forth the praise of God. And it is fitly prefixed to this psalm, where the just man exhorts his soul to the praise of God: because in adversities the soul is sometimes troubled, whether it will or no. Whence above: *Why art thou sad, O my soul, and why dost thou disquiet me?* But that he may take away her disquiet, he suggests joy out of hope, if not out of the thing itself: *Hope in God,* etc. ((AUG.)) This soul, lifted up by hope, praises God here. ((CAS.)) First, he counsels himself, as it were all men, to praise, lest prayer be made among vain things; and as though acquiescing in the counsel, he affirms that he will praise there where he shall be able to praise fully. Secondly, he admonishes others not to hope in man, there: *Trust not.* Thirdly, he teaches that all hope is to be placed in the Almighty, there: *Blessed,* etc.

*Praise the Lord, O my soul.* But it is asked, by whom, and to whom, is this counsel given? If it be said that the flesh counsels the soul, this does not seem to be true, since counsel is wont to be given by the better and the worthier to the inferior: but the flesh is inferior to the soul. For the soul, although it be blamed because it is a sinner, is nevertheless called better by nature than the body that is praised in its own kind, because a spiritual nature excels the body, which it moves, rules, endows with sense, and apprehends: and being itself unbounded, it is near to the substance of God. So gold, blamed because it is foul, surpasses lead in purity, praise *laudatio*; read *laudato*, "that is praised": so too a bad man surpasses the best of horses. Counsel therefore is not given to the soul by the flesh, however greatly it be subdued and made peaceable: which nevertheless is dead because of sin. Nor yet does the mortal flesh counsel the immortal soul, because it is always beneath the soul; but the higher part of the soul, that is, the mind, which thinks upon the divine wisdom, cleaving to it and sighing after it, sees certain of its own parts troubled by the motions of the world, and hurried away to outward things by the desire of earthly goods: whence it calls it back to things inward and higher. Exhorting itself therefore according to its sensuality, it says: *Praise the Lord, O my soul.* For what pleases thee in this world? Divided among so many loves of the things of the ages, gather thyself to thy Author: here is peace and security for thee. Then the soul answers the mind, as one weighed down here and not able to leave off, as is meet. *I will praise in life.* Here in death I shall praise but thinly, because the body *is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the sense that thinketh upon many things ((Sap. IX))*; here hope feeds us, life is in the world to come.

*In my life.* ((CAS.)) When I shall have cleaved to him perfectly, from whom to be parted, as now befalls, is death: but hope consoles, in which, living after a sort, it praises.

*As long as.* Not that at some time he shall not be, because he shall be for ever, and therefore truly long.

*Trust not,* etc. ((CAS.)) The second part. The counsel being given and confirmed, where he shall be able to praise fully, he admonishes them, as though set far off, and in the meantime while evils last (by which the soul is troubled), not to hope in man, but in God. ((AUG.)) Or, as one set in mind at the end of the world: he teaches them not to love things soon to end in place of things eternal; as if by my example also, *trust not,* etc. *In the children of men.* ((ID.)) In one son of man is salvation, and in him do ye hope. Not because he is a son of man, but because he is the Son of God. Not for that which he took from thee, but for that which he kept in himself.
*His spirit shall go forth,* etc. ((CAS.)) First he cleanses hearts by forbidding what is hurtful, that afterward he may aim at what is saving by admonishing to wholesome things.

*Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob.* ((CAS.)) The third part, where he teaches that the whole hope is to be placed in the Almighty, whom he describes from his works, that the Gentile world, so often confuted, may be still. ((AUG.)) Hurtful things being removed, he teaches what belongs to salvation, namely, in whom hope is to be placed. *His helper is his hope.* ((CAS.)) Of that Jacob himself he was so the helper, etc., *as far as* that is, of this true Jacob, as of that one.

*Who made heaven and earth.* ((ID.)) Because the worshippers of demons also have hope in their god, he determines in whom hope ought to be, that is, in Christ, and this he shows even to the end of the psalm, describing him through all things. *All things that are in them.* Lest thou think any other to be the creator, or that there exists a creator even of the smallest things.

*Who keepeth truth for ever.* ((CAS.)) Christ, who is the truth; every man is a liar. *He executeth judgment.* These two pertain to justice. Christ the judge avenges those who suffer for his name, and gives food to them that love him. *For them that suffer wrong.* ((AUG.)) Not every trouble is a wrong. What thou sufferest by right is not a wrong, as is that which the robber and other wicked men suffer. It is one thing therefore to suffer wrong, another to suffer punishment. For a man suffers punishment by right, but wrong is contrary to right.

*The Lord looseth them that are fettered.* ((CAS.)) This belongs to the abundance of his sweetness.

*The Lord lifteth up them that are cast down.* Whom the devil casts down, the Lord lifts up.

*He loveth the just.* ((CAS.)) Whom he sets in eternal blessedness.

*The fatherless and the widow he will receive.* *suseipiet* ((AUG.)) The whole Church of the Gentiles is come as a stranger to the fathers, a daughter not by flesh but by imitation.

*The fatherless* are all who are in pilgrimage, whose father is absent; and every faithful soul is a *widow* while the bridegroom is absent: whence they desire the more both the father and the bridegroom, and God protects them, not seen but desired.

*The Lord shall reign for ever.* ((CAS.)) This is of his magnificence.

He shall reign in us when our hearts shall be firm in him, which is not yet.

notes.text: But godliness with content — The inseparable companion of true, vital religion. Is great gain - Brings unspeakable profit in time, as well as eternity.
Neither can we carry anything out — To what purpose, then, do we heap together so many things? O, give me one thing, - a safe and ready passage to my own country!
Covering — That is, raiment and an house to cover us. This is all that a Christian needs, and all that his religion allows him to desire.

They that desire to be rich — To have more than these; for then they would be so far rich; and the very desire banishes content, and exposes them to ruin. Fall-plunge - A sad gradation! Into temptation - Miserable food for the soul! And a snare - Or trap. Dreadful "covering!" And into many foolish and hurtful desires - Which are sown and fed by having more than we need. Then farewell all hope of content! What then remains, but destruction for the body, and perdition for the soul?

Love of money — Commonly called "prudent care" of what a man has. Is the root - The parent of all manner of evils. Which some coveting have erred - Literally, missed the mark. They aimed not at faith, but at something else. And pierced themselves with many sorrows - From a guilty conscience, tormenting passions, desires contrary to reason, religion, and one another. How cruel are worldly men to themselves!

But thou, O man of God — Whatever all the world else do. A man of God is either a prophet, a messenger of God, or a man devoted to God; a man of another world. Flee - As from a serpent, instead of coveting these things. Follow after righteousness - The whole image of God; though sometimes this word is used, not in the general, but in the particular, acceptation, meaning only that single branch of it which is termed justice. Faith - Which is also taken here in the general and full sense; namely, a divine, supernatural sight of God, chiefly in respect of his mercy in Christ. This faith is the foundation of righteousness, the support of godliness, the root of every grace of the Spirit. Love - This St. Paul intermixes with everything that is good: he, as it were, penetrates whatever he treats of with love, the glorious spring of all inward and outward holiness.

Fight the good fight of faith — Not about words. Lay hold on eternal life - Just before thee. Thou hast confessed the good confession - Perhaps at his baptism: so likewise, ver. 13; but with a remarkable variation of the expression. Thou hast confessed the good confession before many witnesses - To which they all assented. He witnessed the good confession; but Pilate did not assent to it.
I charge thee before God, who quickeneth all things — Who hath quickened thee, and will quicken thee at the great day.
Which — Appearing. In his own times - The power, the knowledge, and the Revelation of which, remain in his eternal mind.
Who only hath underived, independent immortality. Dwelling in light unapproachable — To the highest angel. Whom no man hath seen, or can see - With bodily eyes. Yet "we shall see him as he is."

What follows seems to be a kind of a postscript. Charge the rich in this world — Rich in such beggarly riches as this world affords. Not to be highminded - O who regards this! Not to think better of themselves for their money, or anything it can purchase. Neither to trust in uncertain riches - Which they may lose in an hour; either for happiness or defense. But in the living God - All the rest is dead clay. Who giveth us - As it were holding them out to us in his hand. All things - Which we have. Richly - Freely, abundantly. To enjoy - As his gift, in him and for him. When we use them thus, we do indeed enjoy all things. Where else is there any notice taken of the rich, in all the apostolic writings, save to denounce woes and vengeance upon them?

To do good — To make this their daily employ, that they may be rich - May abound in all good works. Ready to distribute - Singly to particular persons. Willing to communicate - To join in all public works of charity.

Treasuring up for themselves a good foundation — Of an abundant reward, by the free mercy of God. That they may lay hold on eternal life - This cannot be done by alms-deeds; yet they "come up for a memorial before God," Acts x, 4. And the lack even of this may be the cause why God will withhold grace and salvation from us.

glossa.text: *For they that will.* This is said to those who will and are not, that they may not desire. Now to the rich another thing is said, namely, not to be highminded, but to give to the poor. *They fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, because the root of all evils,* etc. There is no kind of evil which does not sometimes arise from covetousness, because the root of all evils is covetousness.

*Covetousness.* In the Greek there stands, φιλαργυρία. If therefore avarice, which properly is the love of money, is taken in place of the genus which is covetousness, a species is put.

*With many sorrows.* For the avaricious sustain the torment of anxiety so much the more, the more they desire the things which either, being had, pass away, or which they cannot have.

*But thou, man,* etc. He does not say that he fears this concerning that man, but he knew that this would come into the hands of the churches. *Flee these things.* For nothing is so harsh and so pernicious as if an ecclesiastical man, and most of all he who holds a lofty place, should give study to the riches of this world: because he harms not only himself but also the rest, to whom he gives a contrary pattern. *Piety.* Piety is that we condescend to the needy, which the covetous man does not do. *Faith.* He who has a true faith concerning God does not desire to become rich amid miseries, nor is the world of more worth to him than God.
*I charge thee.* In Timothy the Apostle speaks to all his successors. *And Christ Jesus.* By the example of Christ he exhorts.
*Blessed and only,* etc. He says this not of the Father only, but of God who is the Trinity itself.

*Who only hath immortality* He has it by nature, others from him by grace. *Inaccessible, whom none of men.* Because none comes to it of himself, but to whom it is given, it is given by his gift, which the Prophet understood, saying: *Come ye to him, and be enlightened ((Psal. XXXIII))*, etc.

*To the rich of this world.* Above he treated of those who wish to become rich, saying that they fall into temptation and the snare of the devil, here he treats of those who are rich, admonishing them not to hope in riches. And because he said that evils come from covetousness, and persuaded the contrary, lest the rich should seem cast off, he determines. *Not to be highminded.* The Apostle did not dread riches, but their disease, that is, pride, which is the worm of the rich. Great is the mind which among riches is not tempted with that disease. He is great who does not therefore think himself great, because he is rich. But he who therefore thinks himself great is proud, is needy, swells in the flesh, cracks in the heart, begs, is puffed up, not full. *To enjoy.* For temporal things God gives in this life to use, eternal things to enjoy: the former, whence we may do good; the latter whence we may be made good.
*To lay up in store.* Unto this are riches sent before that shall not perish.

notes.text: There was a certain rich man — Very probably a Pharisee, and one that justified himself before men; a very honest, as well as honourable gentleman: though it was not proper to mention his name on this occasion: who was clothed in purple and fine linen - and doubtless esteemed on this account, (perhaps not only by those who sold it, but by most that knew him, ) as encouraging trade, and acting according to his quality: And feasted splendidly every day - And consequently was esteemed yet more, for his generosity and hospitality in keeping so good a table.

And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, (according to the Greek pronunciation) or Eleazer. By his name it may be conjectured, he was of no mean family, though it was thus reduced. There was no reason for our Lord to conceal his name, which probably was then well known. Theophylact observes, from the tradition of the Hebrews, that he lived at Jerusalem. Yea, the dogs also came and licked his sores — It seems this circumstance is recorded to show that all his ulcers lay bare, and were not closed or bound up.

And the beggar — Worn out with hunger, and pain, and want of all things, died: and was carried by angels (amazing change of the scene!) into Abraham's bosom - So the Jews styled paradise; the place where the souls of good men remain from death to the resurrection. The rich man also died, and was buried - Doubtless with pomp enough, though we do not read of his lying in state; that stupid, senseless pageantry, that shocking insult on a poor, putrefying carcass, was reserved for our enlightened age!
He seeth Abraham afar off — And yet knew him at that distance: and shall not Abraham's children, when they are together in paradise, know each other!

Father Abraham, have mercy on me — It cannot be denied, but here is one precedent in Scripture of praying to departed saints: but who is it that prays, and with what success? Will any, who considers this, be fond of copying after him?

But Abraham said, Son — According to the flesh. Is it not worthy of observation, that Abraham will not revile even a damned soul? and shall living men revile one another? Thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things - Thou didst choose and accept of worldly things as thy good, thy happiness. And can any be at a loss to know why he was in torments? This damnable idolatry, had there been nothing more, was enough to sink him to the nethermost hell.
Beside this there is a great gulf fixed — Reader, to which side of it wilt thou go?
Lest they also come into this place — He might justly fear lest their reproaches should add to his own torment.
Neither will they be persuaded — Truly to repent: for this implies an entire change of heart: but a thousand apparitions cannot, effect this. God only can, applying his word.

glossa.text:
*A certain man.* Against the avaricious mockers he builds up by an example what he had set forth, namely that the rich man is tormented among those below, who did not make Lazarus his friend, by whom he might have been received into eternal tabernacles; and it seems rather a narrative than a parable.

*Who was clothed in purple,* etc. ((GREG.)) Purple is the colour of royal apparel, from sea-shells, etc., *as far as* because he knew nothing of the bowels of pity, because he was unwilling to redeem the precepts with a price.

*And there was a certain.* If we see anything blameworthy in the poor, we ought not to despise them, because perhaps those whom weakness of manners wounds, the medicine of poverty heals. *Full of sores.* At this man's sores the fastidious rich man shudders, lest amid precious banquets and perfumed guests he should endure the stench of sores with the dogs licking them.

*Desiring.* In one thing two judgments of God are fulfilled: from the sight of the poor man a heap of damnation is brought upon the rich man who does not pity; and again from the sight of the rich man the poor man, tempted daily, is proved, whom, for his own greater proving, poverty together with sickness, and the beheld plenty of the rich man, and no consolation applied to him, afflict. *The dogs.* In the tongue of the dogs there can be signified the tongue of flatterers who lick wounds, while with wicked favour they praise the evils which we blame in ourselves.

*Into Abraham's bosom.* Abraham's bosom is the rest of the blessed poor, whose is the kingdom of heaven, into which after this life they are received. The burial of hell is the depth of punishments, which devours the proud and the unmerciful after this life. *And he was buried.* In the law not niggardliness but rapine is condemned; in the Gospel the rich man is tormented because he did not give what was his own.

*And lifting up.* The unfaithful see afar off, while, set in the depth before the day of judgment, they mark the faithful above them in rest, whose joys afterwards they cannot behold. What they descry is far off, because they do not reach thither by merit.

*He saw Abraham. ((GREG.))* It is to be believed that before the retribution of the last judgment the unjust in rest, etc., *as far as* and they are tormented by the punishment of those whom they loved uselessly.

*That he may dip.* He who did not give to Lazarus the crumbs falling from the table, desires that water be distilled into his mouth from the tip of that man's finger; and he who gave not the least things in life, in hell seeks the least things.

*Because thou hast received. ((AUG.))* Note that this rich man had something of good, out of which he received a transitory good in this life, and Lazarus had something of evil, but the want of fire purged it.

*And in all these things.* Just as the reprobate wish to pass over from their punishments to the glory of the saints, so the just wish in mind through mercy to go to those set in torments, that they may free them; but they cannot, because the souls of the just, though in the goodness of their own nature they have mercy, are yet now joined to the righteousness of their Author and are bound with so great a rectitude that they are moved by no compassion toward the reprobate.

*I beseech thee therefore.* After hope for himself is taken from the burning man, his mind runs back to his kinsmen, because the punishment of the reprobate sometimes uselessly instructs their mind unto charity, so that then at last they love even their own spiritually, who here, while they loved their sins, did not even love themselves. There is kept therefore for the rich man unto punishment both the knowledge of the poor man whom he despised, and the memory of the brethren whom he left behind, that he may be the more tormented by the beheld glory of the despised and by the punishment of those he uselessly loved. *That thou wouldst send.* Too late does this rich man begin to be a master, when he has now neither time for learning nor for teaching.

*If Moses.* They who despise the words of the law, by how much the more subtle the precepts of the Redeemer, who rose from the dead, are, by so much the more hardly will they fulfil these, and him whose sayings they refuse to fulfil, him without doubt they refuse to believe.
